title: The Voynich Manuscript: Message or Nonsense?
intro_title: The Voynich Manuscript: Message or Nonsense?
yt_title: The Voynich Manuscript: The Book Nobody on Earth Can Read
hook: Can a book exist that nobody can read?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, wonder]A painted plant that no botanist can ^name. [act:building the picture]Around it, lines of an alphabet that nobody alive can ^read@present. [p:0.93][act:the number lands][tune:fall]And two hundred and forty pages just like ^it.

[d:tension][act:the child's question, leaning in][tune:rise]Can a book exist that nobody on Earth can ^read@present? [act:plain, the stakes]This one has beaten wartime ^codebreakers, ^computers, and a century of claimed ^solutions. [act:the real puzzle, hushed][tune:rise]Is there a ^message inside at all?

shots.say: The Voynich manuscript: a message, or beautiful nonsense?
shots.draw: The intro title card 'The Voynich Manuscript: Message or Nonsense?' over the dimmed Earth-and-book panel of s3/s4 (no new panel). Only the title is said here.

lines: [d:calm][act:storytelling, unhurried]In {1912|nineteen twelve}, a book dealer called Wilfrid ^Voynich bought a batch of old manuscripts from the Jesuits, near ^Rome. [act:the find, a little wonder][tune:fall]One of them was ^this. [p:0.93][act:the clue, leaning in]And inside it lay a ^letter, written in Prague in about {1665|sixteen sixty-five}.

shots.say: One of them was this. And inside it lay a letter, written in Prague in about 1665.
shots.draw: A long shelf of old manuscript spines (leather browns) builds left to right with a small dealer figure and the tag '1912'; one spine glows gold and slides forward as an open book; a folded letter with lines of Latin handwriting rises out of it, tagged 'Prague, c. 1665'.

lines: [d:build][act:reading the letter, intrigued]Its writer, the physician Johannes Marcus ^Marci, was sending the book to the famous scholar Athanasius ^Kircher, in Rome, [act:the hope, warm][tune:fall]sure that no one else could read@present ^it.

[p:0.93][act:the gossip, savouring it]He passed on a story: the Emperor Rudolf the Second had once paid six hundred ^ducats for it. [p:0.9][act:the punchline][tune:fall]About two kilos of ^gold. [act:fair, a caveat]Second-hand ^gossip. [act:the support, intrigued]But under ultraviolet light, the first page still shows the faded name of the emperor's own ^distiller.

[d:aside][act:tracing it, light][tune:level]And in Kircher's archive sits an older letter, from {1639|sixteen thirty-nine}: [act:the detail][tune:fall]a Prague alchemist, asking for his help with the very same ^book. [act:tracing the chain, light][tune:level]Prague, then Rome, then ^Voynich. [act:the end of the trail][tune:fall]Since {1969|nineteen sixty-nine}, it has lived in Yale's Beinecke ^Library, catalogued as manuscript {408|four oh eight}.

shots.say: Its writer, the physician Johannes Marcus Marci, was sending the book to the famous scholar Athanasius Kircher, in Rome, sure that no one else could read it.
shots.draw: Map of central Europe and Italy (View 4 to 22 E, 39.5 to 52.5 N): gold pin Prague, pin Rome; a small figure at each ('Marci', 'Kircher'); a dotted gold route draws itself from Prague over the Alps to Rome, a tiny book icon riding it; scale bar 300 km.
shots.reuse: voynich shot 2 (the map Prague to Rome), redrawn wide

shots.say: He passed on a story: the Emperor Rudolf the Second had once paid six hundred ducats for it. About two kilos of gold. Second-hand gossip.
shots.draw: A crowned figure ('Rudolf II') and a closed book; 600 small gold coins pop in row by row as a block of 30 by 20 ('600 ducats') with an arrow to the book; two gold bars ('about 2 kg of gold': a ducat held about 3.5 g). On 'Second-hand gossip', a dotted lilac chain from the emperor through three small lilac figures to the letter: claimed, not documented.

shots.say: But under ultraviolet light, the first page still shows the faded name of the emperor's own distiller.
shots.draw: The first page of the book, its text faint; a violet ultraviolet lamp sweeps a beam across it; at the foot of the page a faded line of Latin handwriting glows into view, labelled 'Jacobj a Tepenecz' and 'the emperor's distiller'.

shots.say: And in Kircher's archive sits an older letter, from 1639 ... Prague, then Rome, then Voynich. Since 1969, it has lived in Yale's Beinecke Library, catalogued as manuscript 408.
shots.draw: A timeline 1350 to 2050 builds: a letter icon at 1639 ('a letter to Kircher'); then, as the chain is said, ticks pop: 'Prague, c. 1600' (Rudolf), '1665 to Rome', '1912 Voynich', '1969 Yale, MS 408'; a thin gold thread links them left to right.

lines: [d:build][act:the doubt, fair][tune:rise]But how old is the book ^itself? [act:plain]Some even suspected Voynich of forging ^it.

[p:0.93][act:explaining, the method]In {2009|two thousand nine}, a team at the University of ^Arizona cut four slivers from the edges of its calfskin pages, each about the size of a grain of ^rice. [p:0.93][act:explaining, the analogy]Living things hold a trace of radioactive carbon, which fades after death at a steady pace, like a candle burning ^down: [act:the payoff][tune:fall]measure what's left, and you know when the calf ^died.

[p:0.9][act:the result, plain]Between about {1404|fourteen oh four} and {1438|fourteen thirty-eight}. [act:firm][tune:fall]Not a modern ^fake. [act:the caveat, careful]That dates the ^skin, not the ^ink, [act:fair][tune:fall]but its paints are ordinary pigments of the ^age.

shots.say: But how old is the book itself? Some even suspected Voynich of forging it.
shots.draw: Back on the timeline: a dotted lilac bracket rises over 1912 with a small quill and the words 'forged by Voynich?' (claimed style), and a lilac question mark.

shots.say: In 2009, a team at the University of Arizona cut four slivers from the edges of its calfskin pages, each about the size of a grain of rice.
shots.draw: Four page edges stacked at the left; a scalpel; a small dark notch cut in each edge; on a dark tray at the right, four slivers 1 by 6 mm (drawn at 20 units a millimetre: 120 by 20) with a '6 mm' dimension, beside a grain of rice at the same scale (about 6.5 by 2.5 mm); tag 'Arizona, 2009'.

shots.say: Living things hold a trace of radioactive carbon, which fades after death at a steady pace, like a candle burning down: measure what's left, and you know when the calf died.
shots.draw: A calf silhouette with 16 blue carbon dots; then four candles, tall to short (each lit), with 16, 8, 4 and 2 blue dots above them (the carbon halving as time passes) and an arrow 'time since death' under them; a dimension on the shortest candle: 'what's left tells the date'.

shots.say: Between about 1404 and 1438. Not a modern fake.
shots.draw: Back on the timeline: four sample ticks drop from above onto a gold band 1404 to 1438 that pops and glows, labelled '1404 to 1438, radiocarbon'; the dotted 'forged by Voynich?' bracket is struck through in red.

shots.say: That dates the skin, not the ink, but its paints are ordinary pigments of the age.
shots.draw: Two halves: left, a piece of calfskin with a green tick and a small gold band '1404 to 1438'; right, an ink pot with a dashed outline and a '?' ('ink: not dated'). [p:0.93][act:the point, a smile]It looks like a book of ^herbs, ^heavens and ^healing. [act:the twist, quiet][tune:fall]If only we could read@present the ^labels.

shots.say: So what's in it? Plants, on about half the pages, each with its block of text. Circles of stars, and the signs of the zodiac.
shots.draw: Six small vellum pages in a row, the camera close on the first two (cam z 1.6): a plant page draws itself (plant, block of text); a zodiac page: concentric rings of stars, a ring of small figures, a sign in the centre.

shots.say: Small bathing women in green pools, joined by strange pipes. A fold-out of nine great rosettes.

lines: [d:calm][p:0.93][act:the child's question, curious][tune:rise]How do you study a book you can't ^read@present? [act:plain, a smile][tune:fall]You ^count it. [act:explaining]About thirty-eight thousand ^words, made from some eight thousand different ^ones.

shots.say: You count it. About thirty-eight thousand words, made from some eight thousand different ones.
shots.draw: A grid of 380 small word tiles (19 rows of 20, each tile = 100 words) pops in row by row with a counter label 'about 38,000 words'; then 80 of them turn gold, scattered through the grid, labelled 'about 8,000 different'.

lines: [d:build][p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]In every language, the most common word turns up about twice as often as the ^second, three times as often as the ^third, and so on down a smooth ^staircase. [act:the point, building][tune:fall]This book has the ^same staircase.

[act:one more point, building]And some words crowd into ^one section of the book, the way oven and flour crowd into a ^cookbook. [p:0.93][act:the result]In {2013|twenty thirteen}, two physicists measured that crowding, and found it just like real ^languages: [act:their conclusion, measured][tune:fall]support, they argued, for a genuine ^message.

[d:aside][act:a surprising detail, lightly]In {1976|nineteen seventy-six}, the veteran codebreaker Prescott ^Currier spotted two ^dialects, A and ^B, each with its own favourite ^words. [act:the follow-up, admiring]In {2020|twenty twenty}, the palaeographer Lisa Fagin ^Davis told the handwriting apart, loop by ^loop: [tune:fall]^five scribes. [act:where, explaining]Dialect A runs through most of the plant ^pages; [tune:fall]dialect B, through the bathing ^pools.

shots.say: In every language, the most common word turns up about twice as often as the second ... This book has the same staircase.
shots.draw: Two bar charts side by side, 'English' and 'this book': ten bars each grow from the bottom in rank order (heights 1, 1/2, 1/3 ... of the first: Zipf's law, schematic), a dashed staircase curve draws over each; the second chart's bars wear little Voynich word labels.
shots.reuse: voynich_m 'like a language' scene (the word staircase), redrawn wide

shots.say: And some words crowd into one section of the book, the way oven and flour crowd into a cookbook. In 2013, two physicists measured that crowding ...
shots.draw: Left: a cookbook strip of 12 pages where small 'oven' and 'flour' tags cluster on the baking pages. Right: the Voynich as a strip of sections (plants, stars, pools, recipes); gold dots of one word cluster in one section, blue dots of another in another; label 'Montemurro and Zanette, 2013'.

shots.say: In 1976, the veteran codebreaker Prescott Currier spotted two dialects, A and B, each with its own favourite words.
shots.draw: A long strip of page tiles across the panel (cam on the top half, z 1.35): tiles turn amber (A) or blue (B); above each colour, its own favourite word in Voynich script pops ('A', 'B' chips).

shots.say: In 2020, the palaeographer Lisa Fagin Davis told the handwriting apart, loop by loop: five scribes.
shots.draw: Lower half of the same panel (cam z 1.5): the same gallows letter written five ways (loop size, stem slant, crossbar curve, foot length), each drawing itself above 'scribe 1' to 'scribe 5'; label 'five scribes', 'Davis, 2020'.

shots.say: Dialect A runs through most of the plant pages; dialect B, through the bathing pools.
shots.draw: The whole panel: small section icons (a plant, a pool) appear above the strip; the amber run lines up under the plant icon, the blue under the pools.

[act:puzzled, slower]And words repeat in strange ^runs, the same word two or three times in a row@line, [act:a picture, light][tune:fall]like a stuck ^record@noun.

shots.say: Play a game of guess the next letter. In English, after a q, bet on a u; but most letters keep you guessing. In this book, the next letter is far easier to guess.
shots.draw: Three rows of the game: 'q' with one tall bar for 'u'; 't' with many short bars (h, o, e, i, a, r...); then a Voynich letter with one or two tall bars only. Labels: 'English', 'this book'.
shots.reuse: voynich_m 'unlike a language' scene (the guessing bars), redrawn wide

shots.say: On a standard measure of that surprise, European languages score about three. This book scores about two. A Yale team checked it against nearly three hundred languages, and it matched none.
shots.draw: A bar chart 'surprise per letter': a band of bars at 3.0 to 3.4 ('European languages', Bennett 1976), a lone short bar at 2.2 ('this book') that glows; then a grid of 294 small squares (one per language sample) and the book's square apart, a red 'no match'.

shots.say: And words repeat in strange runs, the same word two or three times in a row, like a stuck record.
shots.draw: A line of Voynich script: the same word appears three times in a row, each copy ringed in amber as it pops; beside it a record on a turntable, the needle jumping back to the same groove.

lines: [d:verdict][act:the landing, even][tune:fall]Word by word, it behaves like a ^language. [act:same rhythm][tune:fall]Letter by letter, like ^none we know.

shots.say: Word by word, it behaves like a language. Letter by letter, like none we know.
shots.draw: Two cards: 'words' with the small staircase and a green tick; 'letters' with the lone 2.2 bar and a red question mark.

lines: [d:build][act:storytelling, relishing it]The first famous solution arrived in {1921|nineteen twenty-one}. [act:introducing him]William ^Newbold, a professor in Philadelphia, said the real message was ^hidden: [act:the claim, vivid][tune:fall]tiny strokes inside each letter, seen only under a ^lens.

[p:0.93][act:his result, wide-eyed]His reading made the English friar Roger ^Bacon the author, with a ^microscope and a ^telescope, [act:the escalation, playful][tune:fall]drawing the spiral of a galaxy, centuries before any telescope could ^show one.

shots.say: William Newbold, a professor in Philadelphia, said the real message was hidden: tiny strokes inside each letter, seen only under a lens.
shots.draw: One big Voynich letter on vellum; a magnifying lens slides over it; inside the lens, tiny strokes along the letter's edge pop in dotted lilac (claimed), labelled 'hidden shorthand?'.

shots.say: His reading made the English friar Roger Bacon the author, with a microscope and a telescope, drawing the spiral of a galaxy, centuries before any telescope could show one.
shots.draw: All in dotted lilac (claimed): a friar figure labelled 'Roger Bacon, 1200s?'; a microscope and a telescope pop beside him; a spiral draws itself in the sky, labelled 'a galaxy?'; a small time arrow 'centuries before telescopes could show it'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the takedown, firm but fair]In {1931|nineteen thirty-one}, the scholar John ^Manly took a closer ^look. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a picture]The tiny strokes were ^cracks, where the ink had dried on the ^skin. [act:the second flaw][tune:level]And Newbold's method let him shuffle letters until Latin came ^out. [act:the landing, dry][tune:fall]Shuffle freely, and a page can say almost ^anything.

shots.say: In 1931, the scholar John Manly took a closer look. The tiny strokes were cracks, where the ink had dried on the skin.
shots.draw: Back to the lens, closer (cam z 1.5): the dotted strokes turn into a network of fine cracks in the dried ink, drawn solid; the label 'cracks in the ink' replaces the claim.

shots.say: And Newbold's method let him shuffle letters until Latin came out. Shuffle freely, and a page can say almost anything.
shots.draw: Four letter tiles R O M A; below them the same four tiles re-form, row after row, into other Latin words: AMOR, MORA, ORAM, RAMO, each popping in; a label 'same letters, any message'.

lines: [d:build][act:raising the stakes]Then came the ^professionals. [p:0.93][act:explaining, impressed]From {1944|nineteen forty-four}, William ^Friedman, the great American codebreaker, ran a study group of wartime cryptanalysts, [act:the method][tune:fall]with the text punched onto cards for the ^machines. [act:the result, plain][tune:fall]It never ^cracked.

[d:aside][act:the anecdote, delighted]In {1959|nineteen fifty-nine}, Friedman hid his verdict in a footnote, as an ^anagram. [act:the irony, a smile][tune:fall]It began: I put no trust in anagrammatic acrostic ^cyphers. [p:0.93][act:the reveal, slower]Unscrambled after his ^death, it read@past: [act:quoting, measured][tune:fall]an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal ^language.

[act:his idea, explaining]A language built from pure ^logic, where the letters of each word file it into a ^category. [act:the catch, plain][tune:fall]But the first known schemes of that kind come from the sixteen ^hundreds, two centuries after the ^vellum.

shots.say: From 1944, William Friedman ... ran a study group of wartime cryptanalysts, with the text punched onto cards for the machines. It never cracked.
shots.draw: A row of six desks with seated figures; a stack of punched cards grows beside a tabulating machine (a boxy iso cabinet with a glowing slot); '1944' tag; a padlock over the book stays shut.

shots.say: In 1959, Friedman hid his verdict in a footnote, as an anagram ... an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal language.
shots.draw: A journal page with a footnote that types itself: 'I put no trust in anagrammatic acrostic cyphers...'; a sealed envelope pops beside it, tagged 'opened after his death'; it opens and a second line types: 'an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal language'.

shots.say: A language built from pure logic, where the letters of each word file it into a category. But the first known schemes of that kind come from the sixteen hundreds, two centuries after the vellum.
shots.draw: A branching tree of categories (dotted lilac, claimed): 'everything' splits into 'plants', 'stars', 'bodies', each branch ending in a Voynich word whose first letter glows. Below, a timeline 1350 to 1750: the gold vellum band 1404 to 1438 and a tick 1668 ('Wilkins, a philosophical language'); a bracket 'two centuries' between them.

lines: [d:calm][act:the modern parade, light][tune:level]Since then, the solutions keep ^coming: [act:listing them][tune:level]^Hebrew, ^Latin, ^Turkish, a lost ^Romance language. [p:0.93][act:one example, fair]In {2016|twenty sixteen}, a computer program guessed Hebrew, with the letters ^rearranged. [act:quoting, even]Through an online translator, its first sentence came out as: [act:reading it out, plainly][tune:fall]she made recommendations to the priest, man of the house@noun and me and ^people. [act:fair, even][tune:fall]One of its authors called it strange but sensible, and said historians of Hebrew would have to ^judge.

shots.draw: A fan of claim cards, each dotted lilac with a language name, popping in turn: 'Hebrew', 'Latin', 'Turkish', 'lost Romance'.

shots.say: In 2016, a computer program guessed Hebrew, with the letters rearranged ... historians of Hebrew would have to judge.

lines: [d:tension][act:the opposite idea, fair]So maybe there's nothing there to ^read@present. [p:0.93][act:the challenger at full strength]In {2004|two thousand four}, the computer scientist Gordon ^Rugg showed how one person could fill a book like this with ^nonsense.

shots.say: In 2004, the computer scientist Gordon Rugg showed how one person could fill a book like this with nonsense.
shots.draw: One seated figure at a desk under a lamp, writing; beside him a stack of vellum pages grows (fx fill) into a whole book; tag '2004, Gordon Rugg'.

lines: [act:explaining, step by step]Write a table of meaningless ^syllables: beginnings, middles and ^ends. [act:explaining, the trick]Lay a card with windows cut in it over the ^table, and copy what ^shows. [act:explaining, the next step]Slide the card, and copy ^again. [sfx:hit][act:delighted, slower][tune:fall]Out comes something very like ^Voynichese.

[act:his case, fair]Later, he argued, the same method can even mimic the word ^staircase. [act:a second recipe, fair]In {2019|twenty nineteen}, Torsten ^Timm and Andreas ^Schinner offered a simpler one: copy a word from earlier on the page, change a letter or two, and carry ^on. [act:the result][tune:fall]Their simulation mimics many of the book's ^quirks.

shots.say: Write a table of meaningless syllables ... Slide the card, and copy again. Out comes something very like Voynichese.
shots.draw: A table of three columns ('beginnings', 'middles', 'ends') filled with Voynich syllables; a dark card with three windows lands on it (one cell in each column shows through); the three syllables join into a word on a page below; the card slides down a row (a dotted ghost where it was) and a second word appears; then a line of words writes itself.

shots.say: Later, he argued, the same method can even mimic the word staircase. In 2019, Torsten Timm and Andreas Schinner ... Their simulation mimics many of the book's quirks.
shots.draw: A small staircase chart pops with 'Rugg and Taylor, 2016'; then a page where a word is copied from an earlier line with an arrow, one letter changed (that glyph glows), and the copy is copied again down the page, a chain of five.

lines: [d:build][act:the objections, fair][tune:level]The objections came ^quickly. [act:the first][tune:level]A card with windows like that is first described around {1550|fifteen fifty}, a century after the ^vellum. [act:the second, building][tune:fall]Critics doubt a sliding card would crowd words by ^topic, the way the physicists ^found. [act:the third, a smile][tune:rise]And five scribes, keeping two dialects apart, page after page, for ^nothing? [act:dry][tune:fall]That's a lot@amount of discipline for a ^joke.

shots.say: The objections came quickly ... That's a lot of discipline for a joke.
shots.draw: Three objections build left to right: a mini timeline (vellum band 1404 to 1438, the card at 1550, a bracket 'a century'); the section strip with clustered word dots and the grille card beside a '?'; five pens and the two dialect colours, amber and blue, with a dotted '?' 'a joke?'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the experiment, delighted]In {2022|twenty twenty-two}, a Yale team tried the obvious ^experiment. [p:0.93][act:explaining]They asked forty-two volunteers to fill pages with fake, meaningless ^text. [act:the result, intrigued][tune:fall]It came out predictable and repetitive, a lot@amount like this ^book.

[act:the exception, careful]Except in one ^way: [tune:fall]nobody packed certain letters into the start and end of words as tightly as the scribes ^did. [act:the other door, fair]And the same team showed that some ciphers, ones that merge sounds together, make text just as ^predictable.

shots.say: In 2022, a Yale team tried the obvious experiment. They asked forty-two volunteers to fill pages with fake, meaningless text. It came out predictable and repetitive, a lot like this book.
shots.draw: 42 small figures in a grid of 6 rows of 7, each popping with a little page; their pages fill with scribbles; two meters then fill: 'predictable', 'repetitive', each pointer landing beside the book's mark.

shots.say: Except in one way: nobody packed certain letters into the start and end of words as tightly as the scribes did. And the same team showed that some ciphers, ones that merge sounds together, make text just as predictable.

description:
Two hundred and forty pages in an alphabet nobody can read, painted with plants no botanist can name, on calfskin from the early fourteen hundreds. For more than a century, the Voynich manuscript has beaten wartime codebreakers, computers and a parade of claimed solutions.

We follow the book from seventeenth-century Prague to Yale, count what can be counted in a text nobody can read, and weigh the main ideas: a real language in cipher, a language built from logic, beautiful nonsense, and the solutions that keep making headlines. Verdict: Open question.

facts_added.fact: Wilfrid Voynich, a book dealer, acquired the manuscript in 1911 or 1912 from the Jesuits near Rome, in a discreet sale of part of their holdings.
facts_added.source: Zandbergen, voynich.nu (history); Britannica ('from a Jesuit college near Rome')

facts_added.fact: A letter from Johannes Marcus Marci, written in Prague and dated 1665 (or 1666), was found inside the book; Marci sent the book to Athanasius Kircher in Rome, convinced that no one else could read it.
facts_added.source: Britannica; Zandbergen, voynich.nu (the Marci letter); Beinecke MS 408

facts_added.fact: Marci reported, from Dr Raphael (Mnishovsky), that Emperor Rudolf II had paid 600 ducats for the book; Marci himself suspended judgement on Roger Bacon as author.
facts_added.source: Marci letter (Beinecke MS 408), as quoted by Zandbergen, voynich.nu

facts_added.fact: 600 ducats is about 2 kg of gold (a ducat held about 3.5 g of gold).
facts_added.source: Arithmetic on the standard ducat weight; Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript' note: 600 ducats = 67.5 troy ounces, about 2.10 kg

facts_added.fact: The name 'Jacobj a Tepenecz' at the foot of the first page, legible under ultraviolet light: Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec, whom Rudolf II ennobled and appointed his imperial distiller.
facts_added.source: Zandbergen, voynich.nu (history); Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript'

facts_added.fact: Georg Baresch, a Prague alchemist, wrote to Kircher in April 1639 about the book (having sent him a sample transcription earlier); the letter survives in Kircher's correspondence in Rome.
facts_added.source: Zandbergen, voynich.nu (history)

facts_added.fact: After Voynich's death the book passed to Ethel Voynich and Anne Nill; H. P. Kraus bought it in 1961 and gave it to Yale in 1969, where it is Beinecke MS 408.
facts_added.source: Zandbergen, voynich.nu (history); Beinecke Library

facts_added.fact: Some suspected Voynich himself of forging the manuscript.

In 2009 the University of Arizona (Greg Hodgins) dated four samples, each about 1 by 6 mm, cut from the edges of four pages; the parchment dates to between 1404 and 1438 (announced 2011). The dating applies to the parchment, not the writing; the inks cannot be dated directly.
facts_added.source: University of Arizona news release 2011 (via Medievalists.net); Zandbergen, voynich.nu (radiocarbon)

facts_added.fact: Analysis by McCrone Associates found the paints to be materials expected of the period (azurite blue, red ochre, copper-based green).
facts_added.source: McCrone Associates 2009, via Zandbergen, voynich.nu and Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript'

facts_added.fact: The sections: herbal (about half the pages), astronomical with zodiac roundels, 'balneological' (small nude women in pools joined by tubes), the cosmological fold-out of nine rosettes, pharmaceutical (jars beside plant parts), and recipes (short paragraphs each marked with a star).
facts_added.source: Britannica; Clemens 2016; Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript' (126 herbal pages of about 240)

facts_added.fact: The text has 37,919 word tokens and 8,114 word types.
facts_added.source: Reddy & Knight 2011 (LaTeCH), as cited by Zandbergen, voynich.nu (word statistics)

facts_added.fact: Word frequencies follow Zipf's law: the most common word occurs about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third.
facts_added.source: Montemurro & Zanette 2013, PLOS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0066344; Reddy & Knight 2011 (LaTeCH)

facts_added.fact: Content words cluster in particular sections, as keywords do in real texts; the authors argue this supports a genuine message and limits the hoax hypothesis.
facts_added.source: Montemurro & Zanette 2013, PLOS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0066344

facts_added.fact: Prescott Currier (1976) identified two 'languages', A and B, with substantially different common vocabulary: A in the herbal and pharmaceutical sections, B in the balneological section and other parts.
facts_added.source: Currier 1976 in D'Imperio 1978; Bowern & Lindemann 2021, doi:10.1146/annurev-linguistics-011619-030613

facts_added.fact: Lisa Fagin Davis (2020) identified five scribes from small differences in letter forms (loops, crossbars, feet), varying between sections but not within them.
facts_added.source: Davis 2020, Manuscript Studies 5(1): 164-180, doi:10.1353/mns.2020.0011

facts_added.fact: Second-order character entropy (h2): Voynich about 2.2 bits, against 3.0 to 3.4 for European languages.
facts_added.source: Bennett 1976, as tabulated by Zandbergen, voynich.nu (character statistics)

facts_added.fact: Compared with 294 language samples, Voynichese is distinct from every comparison text in character predictability.
facts_added.source: Lindemann & Bowern 2020, arXiv:2010.14697

facts_added.fact: Words repeat in runs, the same word two or three times in a row.
facts_added.source: Short 'voynich' (films/rewrite/voynich.json); Bowern & Lindemann 2021

facts_added.fact: William Romaine Newbold (University of Pennsylvania) presented his solution in 1921: microscopic shorthand strokes inside each letter; it made Roger Bacon the author, with a microscope and telescope, and read one drawing as the Andromeda nebula with spiral structure.
facts_added.source: Newbold 1928, The Cipher of Roger Bacon; Zandbergen, voynich.nu (solvers)

facts_added.fact: John Manly (1931) showed the strokes were cracks in the dried ink on the vellum, and that Newbold's method rearranged letters at will.
William Friedman's First Study Group (1944 to 1946) transcribed the text onto IBM punched cards.
facts_added.source: D'Imperio 1978; Zandbergen, voynich.nu (solvers); Reeds 1995, Cryptologia 19(1): 1-23

facts_added.fact: Friedman's 1959 footnote anagram ('I put no trust in anagrammatic acrostic cyphers, for they are of little real value, a waste, and may prove nothing. Finis.') was solved, after his death, as 'The Voynich MSS was an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal language of the a priori type. Friedman.'
facts_added.source: Friedman & Friedman 1959, Philological Quarterly 38: 1-20; Tablet Magazine 2013

facts_added.fact: Philosophical (a priori) languages such as Wilkins's (1668) postdate the manuscript's parchment by about two centuries; no one has assigned a plausible meaning to any Voynich prefix or suffix.
facts_added.source: Wilkins 1668; Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript' (constructed language hypothesis)

facts_added.fact: Claimed solutions include Hebrew, abbreviated Latin, Old Turkic and a 'proto-Romance' language; none has been accepted by specialists.
facts_added.source: Zandbergen, voynich.nu (solvers); Wikipedia 'Voynich manuscript' (decipherment claims 2014 to 2020)

facts_added.fact: Hauer and Kondrak's algorithm (2016) suggested Hebrew written as alphagrams; the first sentence, passed through Google Translate, read 'She made recommendations to the priest, man of the house and me and people'; Kondrak called it a strange sentence to start a manuscript but one that makes sense, and said historians of Hebrew were needed.
facts_added.source: Hauer & Kondrak 2016, TACL 4: 75-86, doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00084; University of Alberta news, January 2018

facts_added.fact: Gordon Rugg (2004) produced Voynich-like text with a table of prefixes, middles and suffixes and a Cardan grille; the grille was described around 1550.
facts_added.source: Rugg 2004, Cryptologia 28(1): 31-46, doi:10.1080/0161-110491892755; Rugg 2004, Scientific American 291(1)

facts_added.fact: Rugg and Taylor (2016) argued the table-and-grille method reproduces Zipf's law and textual clustering.
Timm and Schinner proposed 'self-citation': scribes copying and modifying earlier words; their simulation reproduces many of the text's statistical features.

In a Yale experiment, 42 volunteers wrote pages of meaningless text; it showed lower information content, lower conditional entropy and more repetition, like the Voynich text, but not its strong bias in where characters sit within words.
facts_added.source: Gaskell & Bowern 2022, CEUR Workshop Proceedings 3313

facts_added.fact: Encipherment methods that merge phonemic contrasts can reproduce Voynich-like word-level metrics.
facts_added.source: Bowern & Gaskell 2022, CEUR Workshop Proceedings 3313; Lindemann & Bowern 2020

facts_added.fact: Greshko's Naibbe cipher (2025): dice respace Latin or Italian plaintext into single letters and pairs; playing cards pick one of six substitution tables; the output resembles Voynichese; the author says it is almost certainly not how the manuscript was made, and its replication of Voynich B is incomplete.
facts_added.source: Greshko 2025, Cryptologia, doi:10.1080/01611194.2025.2566408; Newsweek, December 2025; Schneier on Security, December 2025

facts_added.fact: Multispectral images of the first page (taken 2014 by the Lazarus Project and RIT, released 2024) show three columns of letters in the right margin, two in the Roman alphabet and one in Voynich script, probably by Marci.
facts_added.source: The Art Newspaper, 25 September 2024 (L. F. Davis)

end_line: About six hundred years on, its plants are still waiting for a reader.
